<reason>Side A won a competitive, high-quality debate. A's decisive path was threefold: (1) the motion's own text — "most wasteful items," "some inconvenience and transition costs" — pre-absorbed much of B's burden argument, and A exploited this framing well; (2) A anchored its case in concrete, plausible precedents (bag bans, deposit-return bottle systems, France's dine-in restrictions) while B remained almost purely analytic; (3) under pressure, B conceded it had no measured evidence that pricing alone shrinks volumes, while A's own concession (continued use after charges isn't automatic failure) was recovered from cleanly. B's strongest material — the lifecycle substitution argument and the charge that A's "safety valve" was circular — was genuinely damaging, and B's honesty about lacking volume evidence was epistemically creditable. But B's core strategy reframed the motion as "phase-out versus the best less-restrictive alternative," imposing a comparative burden the proposition doesn't clearly carry, and A's closing turn — that B's own stated threshold for a justified phase-out roughly matches what the motion targets, leaving only a dispute about where the line sits — narrowed the debate to A's favor. B's rebuttal that the conditional concession "is not a policy endorsement" was a fair parry but left B defending a status quo priced "forever" without affirmative evidence. Both sides executed the A1/A2 format properly and avoided fake sourcing. A's "renting the harm, not ending it" crystallization was the more memorable and decisive weighing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The pressure-question exchange: B asked what evidence of return rates and costs must precede a phase-out, and A answered with the bag-ban/deposit precedent plus the sharp point that demanding perfect data first is "a veto dressed as prudence." Symmetrically, A's Q1 forced B to admit (in Rebuttal 2) it had no measured estimate that pricing reduces volumes, only a mechanism — a concession A converted into "charges reward lighter single-use, not less single-use," the debate's most damaging landed blow.</best_rebuttal>
